title: Lemon & poppy seed bar soap
subtitle: A light citrus bar with gentle exfoliation
excerpt: Cold-process bar soap scented with lemon essential oil and studded with poppy seeds for a mild scrub finish. Made on an olive and coconut base with a 5% superfat. Yields seven standard bars; hardens over 4-6 weeks.
sourceNotes: Susan Miller Cavitch, The Soapmaker's Companion (1997), lemon EO usage rate in cold-process soap and acceleration risk. Soap-Calc SAP table (accessed 2026), NaOH values: coconut oil 0.190, olive oil 0.134. USDA AAS oil-fatty-acid data for coconut and olive compositions. Note on citrus EOs in CP soap: high-limonene EOs can accelerate trace; stir in at the last moment rather than blending.

recipe.batchNotes: Recalculate lye if you change the oil ratio. Lemon EO can accelerate trace, do not increase the EO percentage above 3% of oil weight.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Bars improve with a longer cure. Make a batch at least 6 weeks before you want to use them.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: 2 years in a cool, dry place. Citrus EOs fade within the first year; the soap remains effective longer but the scent lightens. Discard if orange spots (DOS) or sharp rancid smell develops.

glossaryTerms.definition: The point at which the soap batter thickens enough to hold a trail on its surface when drizzled from a spoon, the signal that emulsification is underway and the batter is ready to mould.
The reaction between fat and lye (sodium hydroxide) that produces soap and glycerol. Each oil has a SAP value, the grams of NaOH needed to saponify one gram of that oil.
The percentage of oil deliberately left unsaponified in a finished bar. A 5% superfat leaves enough free fatty acids to make the bar conditioning rather than stripping.

content.text: Lemon and poppy seed soap is a bright, clean-scented bar on an olive and coconut base, with poppy seeds stirred through for a gentle scrub texture. The coconut oil gives a firm bar with big bubbles; the olive conditions the skin. The lemon essential oil fades slowly over the cure period but the bar keeps its character. Makes seven bars; they're ready in 4-6 weeks.
Ingredients

items.prepNote: pure (not extra virgin); 60% of oil weight; conditioning base
40% of oil weight; lather and hardness
NaOH at 99% purity; calculated for 5% superfat
32% of oil weight; the lye solution liquid
3% of oil weight; stir in at light trace, not blended in; may fade slightly in cure
gentle exfoliant; stir in with the lemon EO at trace

content.text: Method
Make the lye solution
Put on protective gloves and goggles. Work near an open window.
Weigh the distilled water into the HDPE pitcher. Slowly pour the lye into the water, not the other way around. Stir until dissolved. The solution heats sharply; set it aside to cool to 38-42°C.
Prepare the oils
Melt the coconut oil gently, then combine with the olive oil. Both the oil blend and lye solution should be at 38-42°C before combining.
Blend to trace and add fragrance
Pour the lye solution into the oils in a thin stream. Use the stick blender in short 5-second bursts until the batter reaches a light
trace
, it holds a faint trail on the surface.
Switch off the blender. Stir in the lemon essential oil by hand, lemon EO can accelerate trace sharply if blended. Stir in the poppy seeds.
Pour immediately into the silicone mould. Insulate with a towel and leave for 24-48 hours.
Unmould, cut, and cure
Unmould when firm. Cut into 7 bars wearing gloves, fresh soap is still caustic.
Cure on a rack for 4-6 weeks, turning every 2 weeks. The
saponification
is complete when a corner touched to the tongue gives no zap.
Storage and shelf life

Keep cured bars on a draining soap dish in use; store the rest on a ventilated rack in a cool, dry cupboard. The lemon scent fades within a year but the bar lasts 2 years before any risk of rancidity. Discard if orange spots appear on the cut face or the bar smells sharp and oily rather than citrus-clean. The
superfat
oils keep the bar conditioning even once the scent has lightened.
